classification.difficultyReason: The student must identify the inset triangle of permissible centres, connect its offset to the original inradius, and use similarity to obtain an area probability.

content.prompt: A coin of radius $1\text{ cm}$ is tossed onto a plane surface that has been tiled entirely by right triangles whose sides are $8\text{ cm}$, $15\text{ cm}$, and $17\text{ cm}$ long. What is the probability that the coin lands entirely within one of the triangles?

answer.short:
$\dfrac49$.

The coin's centre must lie in the smaller triangle formed by moving each side inward by $1\text{ cm}$; its area is $\dfrac49$ of the original area.
answer.worked:
The coin lies entirely within a triangle when its centre is at least $1\text{ cm}$ from every side. The permissible region is a smaller, similar triangle.

Let $A$, $s$ and $r$ be the area, semiperimeter and inradius of the original triangle.
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac12\times8\times15=60\text{ cm}^2\\s&=\frac{8+15+17}{2}=20\text{ cm}\\r&=\frac{A}{s}=\frac{60}{20}=3\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Moving each side inward by $1\text{ cm}$ reduces the inradius to $2\text{ cm}$, so the smaller triangle has linear scale factor $\dfrac23$.
$$\begin{align*}\Pr(\text{coin entirely within a triangle})&=\frac{\text{permissible area}}{\text{triangle area}}\\\Pr(\text{coin entirely within a triangle})&=\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac49.\end{align*}$$
